title: Bougainville's Voyage Round the World
intro: In 1766 Louis XV gave Bougainville permission to circumnavigate the globe. He sailed with two ships, the Boudeuse and the Étoile. It was the first expedition to circumnavigate the globe with professional naturalists and geographers aboard.
ending: The expedition completed its circumnavigation at Saint-Malo on 16 March 1769, having lost only seven of its 340 crew. Bougainville published his journal in 1771, and its account of Tahitian society was a sensation.

stops.text: Bougainville left Nantes with two ships, the Boudeuse under Nicolas Pierre Duclos-Guyot and the Étoile under François Chenard de la Giraudais. The crews numbered 214 aboard the Boudeuse and 116 aboard the Étoile.
stops.quote: Bougainville left Nantes on 15 November 1766 with two ships: Boudeuse (captain : Nicolas Pierre Duclos-Guyot) and the Étoile (commanded by François Chenard de la Giraudais). This was a large expedition, with a crew of 214 aboard Boudeuse and 116 aboard Étoile.

stops.text: After sighting islands of the Tuamotu group on 22 March, Bougainville saw the peak of Mehetia on 2 April. He then went on to Tahiti.
stops.quote: He saw islands of the Tuamotu group on the following 22 March, on 2 April saw the peak of Mehetia and visited the island of Otaheite shortly after.

stops.text: Bougainville visited Tahiti, where the British captain Samuel Wallis had made a visit and claim less than a year before. He claimed the island for France and named it New Cythera. Jeanne Barret, Commerçon's valet, was found to be a woman and confessed.
stops.quote: He narrowly missed becoming their discoverer; a previous visit and claim had been made by British explorer Samuel Wallis in HMS Dolphin less than a year previously. Bougainville claimed the island for France and named it New Cythera. During this part of his expedition, one of his crew members, Jeanne Barret, was discovered to be a woman and confessed.

stops.text: The expedition left Tahiti and sailed west past southern Samoa and the New Hebrides. On sighting Espiritu Santo it turned west, still looking for the Southern Continent.
stops.quote: His expedition left Tahiti and sailed westward to southern Samoa and the New Hebrides, then on sighting Espiritu Santo turned west still looking for the Southern Continent.

stops.text: The ships sailed through the Solomon Islands but, because of the hostility of the people there, did not land. Bougainville named Bougainville Island for himself.
stops.quote: He sailed through what is now known as the Solomon Islands but, because of the hostility of the people there, avoided landing. He named Bougainville Island for himself.

stops.text: People from New Ireland attacked the expedition, and the French then made for the Moluccas.
stops.quote: The expedition was attacked by people from New Ireland so the French expedition made for the Moluccas.

stops.text: At Batavia the expedition received news that Wallis and Carteret had reached Tahiti before Bougainville.
stops.quote: At Batavia, they received news of Wallis and Carteret who had preceded Bougainville in discovering Tahiti.

stops.text: The expedition completed its circumnavigation here. It had lost only seven of its 340 crew. Bougainville brought with him Ahutoru, a Tahitian who had volunteered to come.
stops.quote: On 16 March 1769, the expedition completed its circumnavigation and arrived at Saint-Malo. It had lost only seven of its 340 crew, an extremely low level of casualties.

notes: Biography: only the circumnavigation is told. The article gives no year for the Tuamotu sighting (22 March), Mehetia (2 April) or Tahiti; 1768 is inferred from the sequence between 1766 and 1769 (article says only 'the following 22 March'). Tahiti has no day; 'April 1768' follows from 'shortly after' 2 April. Dates for Espiritu Santo to Batavia are '1768' by inference; article gives none. Left out: the Tuamotus, southern Samoa and the New Hebrides (island groups, no point), the Moluccas (region), Río de la Plata 31 January 1767 (the article gives it as the Falklands handover, not the voyage), the Falklands settlement (earlier expedition). The article's crew figures disagree: 214+116 aboard at departure, 340 at the end. Batavia is present-day Jakarta (entry jakarta); the article does not say so.
